questions.sub: Classification and Properties of Sensory Receptors
questions.q: According to Sherrington's functional classification of sensory receptors, how do exteroceptors, interoceptors (visceroceptors), and proprioceptors differ?
options: External stimuli, visceral changes and body position
Only stimuli within cerebral ventricles
Light and sound only
Directly innervating skeletal muscle fibres
questions.explain: Sherrington grouped receptors by stimulus source: external world (exteroceptors), internal viscera (interoceptors), and musculoskeletal position/kinesthesia (proprioceptors).

open.q: Define exteroceptors, interoceptors, and proprioceptors, giving two specific examples of each.
accept: Exteroceptors: external stimuli (cutaneous mechanoreceptors, thermoreceptors, photoreceptors); Interoceptors: internal visceral environment (arterial baroreceptors, carotid chemoreceptors, hypothalamic osmoreceptors); Proprioceptors: body position and movement (muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, joint capsule receptors)
External surface receptors (touch/temperature), visceral receptors (baroreceptors/osmoreceptors), musculoskeletal position receptors (muscle spindles/Golgi tendon organs)

questions.sub: Classification and Properties of Sensory Receptors
questions.q: What is 'Muller's law of specific nerve energies' (the labeled-line principle)?
options: Sensation depends on the specific afferent pathway and cortex activated
All sensory receptors fire identical action potentials at 1,000 Hz
Action potential amplitude doubles when stimulus intensity doubles
A single afferent axon simultaneously carries pain, vision, hearing
questions.explain: Because action potentials are all-or-none electrical events identical in form across neurons, modality specificity is encoded anatomically by which central pathway and primary sensory cortex receives the input.

open.q: State Muller's law of specific nerve energies (labeled-line coding) and give an everyday example.
accept: Stimulation of a specific sensory receptor or afferent pathway always evokes the characteristic sensation of that pathway regardless of the stimulus modality (e.g., mechanical pressure on the eye evokes light flashes/phosphenes)
Modality is determined by the specific neural pathway and cortical destination activated rather than the nature of the stimulus

questions.sub: Sensory Transduction, Receptor Potential, and Adaptation
questions.q: How does a 'receptor potential' (generator potential) differ from an 'action potential' in a sensory neuron?
options: Graded, local, summating, amplitude-codes intensity; decaying, non-propagated
All-or-none, propagates unchanged to the thalamus without decrement
Amplitude varies with stimulus while receptor potentials are fixed
Always hyperpolarizes mechanoreceptors during sustained stimulation
questions.explain: In Pacinian corpuscles, mechanical deformation opens stretch-sensitive cation channels (Na+ influx) at the unmyelinated nerve ending, generating a graded receptor potential that triggers action potentials at the first node of Ranvier.

open.q: Contrast four biophysical properties of a sensory receptor potential versus an axonal action potential.
accept: Receptor potential: graded amplitude, decremental/non-propagated, lacks a refractory period (can summate), encodes intensity by amplitude; Action potential: all-or-none, self-propagating, has an absolute refractory period, encodes intensity by firing frequency
Graded/local/summating (receptor potential) vs all-or-none/propagated/refractory (action potential)

questions.sub: Sensory Transduction, Receptor Potential, and Adaptation
questions.q: What is the 'Weber-Fechner law' of sensory intensity coding?
options: Perceived intensity is proportional to log(stimulus intensity)
Perceived sensation decreases to zero as intensity increases
Action potential velocity is inversely proportional to axon diameter
Two-point discrimination is identical on fingertips and back
questions.explain: Logarithmic compression (and Stevens' power law) explains why adding 1 candle in a dark room is dramatically noticeable, whereas adding 1 candle in bright sunlight is barely perceptible.

open.q: State the mathematical relationship and physiological advantage of the Weber-Fechner law.
accept: Perceived sensation intensity is proportional to the logarithm of stimulus intensity; provides high sensitivity at low stimulus levels while spanning a wide dynamic range of intensities
Sensation proportional to log(stimulus intensity); allows wide dynamic range without receptor saturation

questions.sub: Sensory Transduction, Receptor Potential, and Adaptation
questions.q: How do 'phasic' (rapidly adapting) receptors and 'tonic' (slowly adapting) receptors differ in their firing patterns and physiological functions?
options: Phasic receptors respond to change; tonic receptors maintain firing
Tonic receptors adapt rapidly; phasic receptors never adapt
Nociceptors are the fastest-adapting receptors
Pacinian corpuscles are non-adapting tonic receptors
questions.explain: In the Pacinian corpuscle, concentric fluid-filled connective tissue lamellae redistribute mechanical pressure within milliseconds, dissipating the static deformation on the central neurite so it responds purely to rapid vibration (200-300 Hz).

open.q: Compare phasic (rapidly adapting) and tonic (slowly adapting) receptors, giving two examples and the primary functional role of each.
accept: Phasic receptors (Pacinian corpuscles, Meissner corpuscles) adapt rapidly to constant stimuli and signal change/velocity/vibration; Tonic receptors (muscle spindles, nociceptors, arterial baroreceptors, Merkel discs) fire persistently during sustained stimuli to signal continuous state/position/danger
Rapidly adapting signaling change/vibration (Pacinian, Meissner) vs slowly adapting signaling sustained state (muscle spindles, nociceptors, baroreceptors)

questions.sub: Cutaneous Mechanoreceptors and Somatosensory Coding
questions.q: Match the four major cutaneous tactile mechanoreceptors of glabrous (hairless) skin with their correct receptive field size and adaptation rate:
options: Meissner: small, rapid; Merkel: small, slow; Pacinian: large, rapid; Ruffini: large, slow
Pacinian: tiny, non-adapting; Merkel: huge, fast-adapting fields
Meissner: deep, slow; Ruffini: superficial, fast-adapting endings
All four receptors have identical fields and adaptation rates
questions.explain: Superficial receptors (Meissner, Merkel) have small, sharp receptive fields for high spatial acuity (fingertips), whereas deep dermal/subcutaneous receptors (Pacinian, Ruffini) have large receptive fields for vibration and skin stretch.

open.q: State the receptive field size (small vs large) and adaptation rate (rapid vs slow) for: (1) Meissner corpuscles, (2) Merkel discs, (3) Pacinian corpuscles, and (4) Ruffini endings.
accept: Meissner: small, rapid; Merkel: small, slow; Pacinian: large, very rapid; Ruffini: large, slow
1) Small/rapid, 2) Small/slow, 3) Large/rapid, 4) Large/slow

questions.sub: Cutaneous Mechanoreceptors and Somatosensory Coding
questions.q: What is 'lateral inhibition' in somatosensory relay nuclei (dorsal column nuclei, thalamus, and somatosensory cortex), and how does it enhance spatial acuity?
options: Excited neurons inhibit nearby weakly active neurons, sharpening contrast
Left-hand stimulation blocks all right-hand sensation
Lateral inhibition removes all central action potentials
It enlarges receptive fields tenfold
questions.explain: Lateral inhibition sharpens spatial borders in tactile localization, vision (horizontal/amacrine cells), and auditory pitch discrimination.

open.q: Explain the circuit mechanism and perceptual benefit of lateral inhibition in somatosensory pathways.
accept: Strongly activated central sensory neurons excite inhibitory interneurons that suppress neighboring less-active neurons, sharpening center-surround contrast and enhancing spatial localization / two-point discrimination
Inhibition of surrounding neurons by the most active central neuron to sharpen spatial contrast and acuity

questions.sub: Nociceptors, Thermoreceptors, and Pain Modulation
questions.q: How do 'fast (first) pain' and 'slow (second) pain' differ in their afferent nerve fiber types, conduction velocities, neurotransmitters, and perceptual qualities?
options: Fast: myelinated A-delta, glutamate, sharp pricking; slow: unmyelinated C, substance P, dull burning
Fast: unmyelinated C fibers, slow conduction; slow: myelinated A-alpha fast fibers
Both fast and slow pain are carried by large myelinated A-beta fibers
Slow pain uses acetylcholine as its transmitter at the neuromuscular junction
questions.explain: Stubbing a toe produces an immediate sharp A-delta prick followed ~1 second later by a throbbing, diffuse C-fiber ache.

open.q: Compare fast pain and slow pain in terms of nerve fiber type, myelination, conduction velocity, and quality of sensation.
accept: Fast pain: myelinated A-delta fibers (~5-30 m/s), sharp/pricking/well-localized; Slow pain: unmyelinated C fibers (~0.5-2 m/s), dull/burning/aching/poorly localized
A-delta myelinated/fast/sharp vs C unmyelinated/slow/dull burning

questions.sub: Nociceptors, Thermoreceptors, and Pain Modulation
questions.q: What is the 'Gate Control Theory of Pain' (Melzack and Wall), and why does rubbing an injured shin or applying Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (TENS) relieve pain?
options: A-beta input activates inhibitory dorsal-horn interneurons that reduce A-delta/C transmission
Rubbing permanently destroys C fibres
A-beta fibres release systemic morphine
Spinal gating blocks all respiratory motor output
questions.explain: Non-painful tactile input (A-beta) 'closes the gate' in lamina II of the dorsal horn, dampening nociceptive C-fiber signaling to the brain.

open.q: Explain the spinal dorsal horn mechanism of the Gate Control Theory of pain when large A-beta mechanoreceptor fibers are stimulated.
accept: Large myelinated A-beta tactile afferents activate inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) of the dorsal horn, suppressing transmission from A-delta/C pain afferents to spinothalamic projection neurons
A-beta fibers excite dorsal horn inhibitory interneurons that block A-delta/C nociceptive transmission

questions.sub: Nociceptors, Thermoreceptors, and Pain Modulation
questions.q: What is the 'descending endogenous analgesia system', and which brainstem nuclei and neurotransmitters suppress dorsal horn pain transmission?
options: PAG -> raphe magnus (5-HT) and locus coeruleus (NE) -> dorsal horn enkephalin interneurons
Primary motor cortex -> vagus nerve -> acetylcholine release in the skin
Cerebellar Purkinje cells -> histamine release directly into the CSF
Substantia nigra -> dopamine release directly onto skeletal muscle
questions.explain: Endogenous opioids (endorphins, enkephalins, dynorphins), serotonin, and norepinephrine mediate stress-induced analgesia and are mimicked pharmacologically by morphine, tramadol, and SNRIs (duloxetine).

open.q: Outline the descending endogenous pain-suppression pathway from the midbrain to the spinal dorsal horn and name its key neurotransmitters.
accept: Midbrain periaqueductal gray (PAG) activates nucleus raphe magnus (serotonin) and locus coeruleus (norepinephrine), which stimulate dorsal horn enkephalinergic interneurons to inhibit nociceptive transmission
PAG -> nucleus raphe magnus (5-HT) & locus coeruleus (NE) -> dorsal horn enkephalin interneurons

questions.sub: Nociceptors, Thermoreceptors, and Pain Modulation
questions.q: What is the neuroanatomical basis of 'referred pain' (such as myocardial ischemic pain felt in the left arm/shoulder or diaphragmatic irritation felt at the C4 shoulder tip)?
options: Visceral and somatic afferents converge on the same spinothalamic neurons
Visceral organs contain no nerve fibers of any kind whatsoever
Heart pain travels directly through the optic nerve to the cortex
Somatic nerves innervate the myocardium directly via the plexus
questions.explain: For example, central diaphragmatic phrenic afferents (C3-C5) converge on C3-C5 dorsal horn neurons receiving somatic input from the supraclavicular shoulder skin (Kehr's sign).

open.q: Explain the convergence-projection mechanism of referred pain and give one classic clinical example with its spinal cord segments.
accept: Visceral and somatic pain afferents converge onto the same second-order dorsal horn spinothalamic neurons, causing the cortex to localize visceral pain to the corresponding somatic dermatome (e.g., myocardial ischemia T1-T5 referred to left arm/chest, or diaphragm C3-C5 referred to shoulder tip)
Convergence of visceral and somatic afferents on shared dorsal horn neurons (e.g., heart T1-T5 to left arm or diaphragm C3-C5 to shoulder)

questions.sub: Muscle Spindles and the Stretch (Myotatic) Reflex
questions.q: Describe the internal structure, sensory innervation, and motor innervation of a mammalian 'muscle spindle':
options: Intrafusal bag and chain fibers in parallel; Ia and II afferents; gamma motor neurons
In series within tendons; innervated solely by Type Ib afferents without motor
Located in cardiac ventricles; innervated bilaterally by the vagus nerve
Innervated by alpha motor neurons in the central equatorial region only
questions.explain: Because muscle spindles lie in parallel with extrafusal fibers, stretching the whole muscle stretches the central non-contractile equatorial region of intrafusal fibers, opening mechanosensitive channels on Type Ia and II sensory endings.

open.q: State the orientation of muscle spindles relative to extrafusal fibers, their two types of intrafusal fibers, their two sensory afferent fiber types, and their motor nerve supply.
accept: Arranged in parallel with extrafusal fibers; nuclear bag and nuclear chain intrafusal fibers; Type Ia (annulospiral) and Type II (flower-spray) sensory afferents; gamma motor neurons
In parallel; nuclear bag & chain fibers; Type Ia & II afferents; gamma motor neurons

questions.sub: Muscle Spindles and the Stretch (Myotatic) Reflex
questions.q: How do 'nuclear bag fibers' and 'nuclear chain fibers' within the muscle spindle differ in their response to muscle stretch?
options: Bag fibers signal velocity/rate of stretch; chain fibers signal static length
Bag fibers detect only temperature; chain fibers detect only noxious pain
Chain fibers fire exclusively during muscle relaxation and never at rest
Both fiber types are innervated by large myelinated Type Ib afferents
questions.explain: Dynamic nuclear bag fibers fire a brisk burst during rapid stretch (driving phasic deep tendon reflexes like the knee jerk), while static nuclear chain fibers fire steadily to maintain tonic posture.

open.q: Contrast the sensory functions of nuclear bag intrafusal fibers versus nuclear chain intrafusal fibers.
accept: Nuclear bag fibers detect dynamic rate/velocity of muscle stretch (innervated by Type Ia afferents), whereas nuclear chain fibers detect static, sustained muscle length (innervated by Type II and Type Ia afferents)
Dynamic rate of stretch (nuclear bag) vs static muscle length (nuclear chain)

questions.sub: Muscle Spindles and the Stretch (Myotatic) Reflex
questions.q: What is the neural circuit of the 'monosynaptic stretch (myotatic) reflex' (e.g., the patellar tendon reflex), and what is 'reciprocal inhibition'?
options: Ia afferent directly excites the agonist alpha motor neuron and, via an interneuron, inhibits the antagonist
The stretch reflex requires four synapses in the cerebral cortex to complete
Ia afferents inhibit the stretched muscle and simultaneously contract the antagonist
The patellar reflex is mediated by Type Ib afferents and gamma motor neurons alone
questions.explain: The monosynaptic stretch reflex is the ONLY monosynaptic reflex arc in the human body, providing ultra-fast (~20-30 ms) negative-feedback resistance against unwanted muscle lengthening.

open.q: Trace the complete reflex arc of the patellar stretch reflex, including both agonist excitation and antagonist reciprocal inhibition.
accept: Muscle stretch -> spindle Type Ia afferent -> monosynaptic excitatory synapse on quadriceps alpha motor neuron (quadriceps contraction) AND disynaptic excitation of Ia inhibitory interneuron inhibiting antagonist hamstring alpha motor neurons
Stretch -> Type Ia afferent -> direct excitation of agonist alpha motor neuron + Ia inhibitory interneuron suppression of antagonist

questions.sub: Muscle Spindles and the Stretch (Myotatic) Reflex
questions.q: What is 'alpha-gamma coactivation', and why is it physiologically essential during voluntary skeletal muscle contraction?
options: Simultaneous alpha and gamma firing keeps the spindle taut during extrafusal shortening
Alpha motor neurons inhibit gamma motor neurons so the spindle goes silent
Gamma motor neurons directly lift heavy weights without any alpha involvement
Alpha-gamma coactivation occurs only during REM sleep paralysis in adults
questions.explain: Without alpha-gamma coactivation, extrafusal muscle shortening would unload the parallel muscle spindle, causing Type Ia sensory firing to fall silent ('spindle pause') and blinding the CNS to muscle length during movement.

open.q: Define alpha-gamma coactivation and explain what would happen to muscle spindle sensitivity during voluntary contraction without it.
accept: Simultaneous activation of alpha motor neurons (extrafusal contraction) and gamma motor neurons (intrafusal polar contraction); without it, muscle shortening would slacken the parallel spindle and silence Type Ia sensory feedback
Co-stimulation of alpha and gamma motor neurons so intrafusal fibers shorten alongside extrafusal fibers, preventing spindle unloading/silence

questions.sub: Golgi Tendon Organs and the Inverse Stretch Reflex
questions.q: How do 'Golgi tendon organs' (GTOs) differ from muscle spindles in anatomical arrangement, stimulus modality, sensory afferent fiber type, and reflex action?
options: In series at the tendon; detect tension via Type Ib afferents; inhibit the homonymous muscle
In parallel with extrafusal fibers; detect length; cause powerful muscle contraction
Innervated by gamma motor neurons and Type II afferents from the tendon
Detect skin temperature and trigger reflex sweating via sympathetic fibers
questions.explain: When active isometric contraction generates dangerously high tendon tension, collagen strands squeeze intertwined Type Ib endings, triggering disynaptic autogenic inhibition to protect the muscle-tendon unit from avulsion and finely regulate muscle force.

open.q: Contrast muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs in terms of: (1) anatomical arrangement, (2) adequate stimulus, (3) sensory afferent fiber, and (4) reflex effect on the homonymous muscle.
accept: Muscle spindle: in parallel, detects muscle length/velocity, Type Ia/II afferents, excites homonymous muscle; Golgi tendon organ: in series at tendon, detects muscle tension/force, Type Ib afferents, inhibits homonymous muscle (autogenic inhibition)
Spindle (parallel/length/Ia/excitation) vs GTO (in series/tension/Ib/inhibition)

questions.sub: Golgi Tendon Organs and the Inverse Stretch Reflex
questions.q: What is the 'clasp-knife phenomenon' (lengthening reaction) seen on neurological examination in a patient with upper motor neuron spasticity?
options: Initial resistance to passive stretch suddenly gives way as GTO autogenic inhibition engages
Permanent rigid resistance equal throughout all angles of passive movement
Complete flaccid paralysis with zero resistance to passive stretch at any angle
Rhythmic tremor at 4-6 Hz at rest that disappears with voluntary movement
questions.explain: Clasp-knife spasticity is velocity-dependent and reflects hyperexcitable stretch reflexes abruptly overridden by Golgi tendon organ autogenic inhibition, distinguishing UMN spasticity from basal ganglia lead-pipe/cogwheel rigidity.

open.q: Explain the physiological mechanism of the clasp-knife phenomenon in upper motor neuron spasticity.
accept: Initial brisk resistance from a hyperactive stretch reflex abruptly collapses when high muscle tension activates Golgi tendon organ Type Ib afferents, triggering autogenic inhibition of the stretched muscle
Hyperactive stretch reflex resistance suddenly inhibited by Golgi tendon organ autogenic inhibition

questions.sub: Flexor Withdrawal and Crossed-Extensor Reflexes
questions.q: Describe the neural circuit and functional purpose of the 'flexor withdrawal reflex' and the 'crossed-extensor reflex' when stepping on a sharp tack with the right foot:
options: Ipsilateral flexors excited/extensors inhibited; contralateral extensors excited/flexors inhibited
Both legs immediately flex simultaneously, dropping the person onto the tack
It is a monosynaptic reflex involving only Type Ia afferents from the foot
The right leg extends forcefully onto the tack while the left leg flexes
questions.explain: The crossed-extensor reflex takes ~200-500 ms (many polysynaptic interneurons) and exhibits prolonged 'afterdischarge' so postural support persists until the injured limb is safely clear.

open.q: Explain how the flexor withdrawal reflex and crossed-extensor reflex coordinate ipsilateral and contralateral limb muscles when a noxious stimulus strikes one foot.
accept: Polysynaptic nociceptive pathways excite ipsilateral flexors and inhibit ipsilateral extensors (withdrawing the injured limb), while crossing the spinal midline to excite contralateral extensors and inhibit contralateral flexors (supporting body weight)
Ipsilateral flexion/extensor inhibition to withdraw from pain + contralateral extension/flexor inhibition to bear weight

questions.sub: Spinal Cord Interneurons and Renshaw Inhibition
questions.q: What is 'Renshaw cell inhibition' (recurrent inhibition) in the spinal cord ventral horn?
options: Motor axon collaterals excite glycinergic Renshaw cells that inhibit the same motor neurons
Renshaw cells excite gamma motor neurons via epinephrine release into the blood
Renshaw cells transmit pain signals to the thalamus via the spinothalamic tract
Renshaw cells secrete cerebrospinal fluid into the central canal of the cord
questions.explain: Tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin) blocks presynaptic release of glycine and GABA from Renshaw cells and Ia inhibitory interneurons, causing uninhibited alpha motor neuron firing and severe spastic paralysis (trismus/lockjaw, opisthotonos).

open.q: Describe the recurrent inhibitory circuit mediated by Renshaw cells and name the inhibitory neurotransmitter they release.
accept: Alpha motor neuron axon collaterals excite Renshaw cells (via acetylcholine), which in turn inhibit the same and adjacent alpha motor neurons by releasing glycine
Negative-feedback inhibition of alpha motor neurons via glycinergic Renshaw interneurons

questions.sub: General Properties of Reflexes
questions.q: Which of the following are classic physiological properties of polysynaptic spinal reflexes (such as the flexor withdrawal reflex)?
options: Synaptic delay, summation, divergence, afterdischarge, fatigue, habituation
Zero synaptic delay and absolute inability to fatigue under any stimulus
Complete independence from excitatory or inhibitory postsynaptic potentials
Conduction exclusively through unmyelinated autonomic postganglionic fibers
questions.explain: Afterdischarge in reverberating interneuronal circuits keeps the limb withdrawn for several seconds even after a brief pinprick ends.

open.q: Define 'afterdischarge', 'irradiation', and 'synaptic fatigue' in polysynaptic spinal reflexes.
accept: Afterdischarge: continued motor output after sensory stimulus ceases due to reverberating interneuron circuits; Irradiation: spread of reflex excitation to adjacent spinal segments with stronger stimuli; Synaptic fatigue: progressive weakening of reflex response during repetitive stimulation due to neurotransmitter vesicle depletion
Continued firing post-stimulus (afterdischarge), multi-segment spread (irradiation), and vesicle-depletion weakening (fatigue)

questions.sub: Upper vs Lower Motor Neuron Lesions and Spinal Shock
questions.q: What is 'spinal shock' immediately following an acute complete spinal cord transection (e.g., at T6), and how do reflexes evolve weeks later?
options: Initially flaccid areflexia; later spastic hyperreflexia, Babinski, automatic bladder
Immediate extreme spasticity and clonus within the first 10 seconds after injury
Permanent loss of all spinal reflexes forever, with no recovery at any stage
Hyperreflexia above the lesion with normal voluntary walking below the lesion
questions.explain: Recovery of the bulbocavernosus reflex (S2-S4) is typically the first sign that spinal shock is resolving.

open.q: Contrast the motor tone and deep tendon reflexes beneath a complete spinal cord transection during acute 'spinal shock' versus the chronic recovery stage months later.
accept: Acute spinal shock: flaccid paralysis, hypotonia, and areflexia (absent reflexes); Chronic stage: hypertonia/spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and positive Babinski sign
Flaccid areflexia acutely vs spastic hyperreflexia chronically

questions.sub: Upper vs Lower Motor Neuron Lesions and Spinal Shock
questions.q: How do the clinical findings of an Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) lesion differ from a Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) lesion?
options: UMN: spastic, hyperreflexic, no fasciculations; LMN: flaccid, areflexic, fasciculations
UMN causes severe fasciculations and absent reflexes; LMN causes spasticity and Babinski
Both UMN and LMN lesions produce identical flaccid areflexia and severe atrophy
LMN lesions cause clonus and hypertonia; UMN lesions cause severe muscle atrophy
questions.explain: LMN lesions destroy the final common pathway (ventral horn cell or motor axon), denervating skeletal muscle (causing atrophy and spontaneous nicotinic-receptor fasciculations), whereas UMN lesions remove descending cortical inhibition of brainstem/spinal reflex arcs.

open.q: Compare Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) and Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) lesions across four clinical signs: muscle tone, deep tendon reflexes, muscle atrophy, and fasciculations.
accept: UMN: hypertonia/spasticity, hyperreflexia, mild disuse atrophy only, no fasciculations; LMN: hypotonia/flaccidity, hyporeflexia/areflexia, severe rapid atrophy, fasciculations present
Spastic/hyperreflexic/no fasciculations (UMN) vs flaccid/areflexic/severe atrophy/fasciculations (LMN)

questions.sub: Upper vs Lower Motor Neuron Lesions and Spinal Shock
questions.q: What is the 'Babinski sign' (extensor plantar response), and when is it physiological versus pathological?
options: Great toe dorsiflexion with toe fanning; normal in infants, pathological in adults
Plantar flexion of all toes; pathological at every age from birth to adulthood
Dorsiflexion of the great toe; normal in healthy 30-year-old adults on both sides
Extension of the elbow when the biceps tendon is tapped with a reflex hammer
questions.explain: In healthy adults with intact myelinated corticospinal tracts, plantar stimulation produces downward plantar flexion of the toes; UMN lesions unmask the primitive spinal extensor synergy.

open.q: Describe a positive Babinski sign and explain why it is normal in infants but pathological in adults.
accept: Dorsiflexion (upward extension) of the hallux with fanning of the other toes upon stroking the lateral plantar sole; physiological in infants because corticospinal tracts are not yet fully myelinated, and pathological in adults indicating corticospinal (UMN) tract damage
Great toe dorsiflexion and toe fanning; normal in infants due to incomplete corticospinal myelination, abnormal in adults due to UMN lesion

questions.sub: Upper vs Lower Motor Neuron Lesions and Spinal Shock
questions.q: What is 'ankle clonus', and what neural mechanism produces it in patients with upper motor neuron lesions?
options: Rhythmic oscillations from sustained stretch; indicates hyperexcitable stretch reflex
Complete absence of ankle movement when the Achilles tendon is tapped
A pill-rolling tremor at rest that involves only the fingers and wrists
Voluntary tapping of the foot that occurs only while listening to music
questions.explain: Sustained stretch triggers a hyperactive gastrocnemius-soleus stretch reflex contraction that briefly unloads spindles, followed by gravity/examiner dorsiflexion restretching the spindles in a self-sustaining oscillation (>3-4 beats is pathological).

open.q: Define clonus and state what neurological lesion it indicates.
accept: Involuntary rhythmic oscillating muscle contractions triggered by sudden sustained passive stretch; indicates an upper motor neuron (corticospinal) lesion with hyperexcitable stretch reflexes
Rhythmic stretch-induced oscillating contractions caused by UMN lesion hyperreflexia

questions.sub: Clinical Deep Tendon and Superficial Reflexes
questions.q: Match the five standard clinical deep tendon (muscle stretch) reflexes with their primary spinal cord root levels:
options: Biceps C5-C6; Brachioradialis C5-C6; Triceps C7; Patellar L3-L4; Achilles S1
Biceps L4; Patellar C5; Achilles T10; Triceps T4; Brachioradialis S2
Triceps S1; Achilles C7; Biceps L2; Patellar T1; Brachioradialis L5
All five reflexes are mediated by the first and second cervical roots (C1-C2)
questions.explain: Mnemonic ascending from ankle to elbow: S1,2 (Achilles), L3,4 (Patellar), C5,6 (Biceps/Brachioradialis), C7,8 (Triceps) — '1-2 buckle my shoe, 3-4 kick the door, 5-6 pick up sticks, 7-8 lay them straight.'

open.q: State the primary spinal nerve root levels tested by: (1) biceps reflex, (2) triceps reflex, (3) patellar reflex, and (4) Achilles reflex.
accept: Biceps: C5-C6; Triceps: C7; Patellar: L2-L4 (L3-L4); Achilles: S1 (S1-S2)

questions.sub: Clinical Deep Tendon and Superficial Reflexes
questions.q: What is the 'Jendrassik maneuver' (e.g., hooking fingers together and pulling hard while the examiner taps the patellar tendon), and how does it reinforce weak deep tendon reflexes?
options: Remote muscle contraction raises descending gamma drive, enhancing spindle sensitivity
It paralyzes the hamstring muscles with local anesthetic injected at the tendon
It blocks the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway at the level of the medulla
It directly stimulates the femoral nerve mechanically through the skin of the thigh
questions.explain: Jendrassik reinforcement distinguishes true organic areflexia (e.g., peripheral neuropathy/radiculopathy, where the reflex remains absent) from normal physiologic hyporeflexia.

open.q: Explain the physiological mechanism by which the Jendrassik maneuver enhances deep tendon reflexes.
accept: Forceful voluntary contraction of remote muscles increases descending facilitation of spinal gamma motor neurons and reduces Ia presynaptic inhibition, heightening muscle spindle sensitivity
Increases generalized gamma motor neuron fusimotor drive and reduces Ia presynaptic inhibition

questions.sub: Clinical Deep Tendon and Superficial Reflexes
questions.q: Identify the afferent and efferent cranial/spinal nerves for the corneal, pupillary light, and gag reflexes:
options: Corneal V1/VII; pupillary II/III; gag IX/X
Corneal II/XII; gag I/IV; pupillary V/VI
Pupillary light reflex uses afferent CN V and efferent CN VI, not II/III
All three reflexes are mediated purely by the cervical spinal nerves C1-C4
questions.explain: Because all three brainstem reflexes project bilaterally to efferent nuclei, unilateral afferent lesions abolish both direct and consensual responses on that side, whereas unilateral efferent lesions abolish only the ipsilateral motor response.

open.q: State the afferent and efferent cranial nerves for: (1) the corneal blink reflex, (2) the pupillary light reflex, and (3) the gag reflex.
accept: 1) Corneal: afferent CN V1, efferent CN VII; 2) Pupillary light: afferent CN II, efferent CN III; 3) Gag: afferent CN IX, efferent CN X
V1/VII, II/III, IX/X

questions.sub: Sensory Transduction, Receptor Potential, and Adaptation
questions.q: In vertebrate retinal rod and cone photoreceptors (an unusual exception among sensory receptors), how does light stimulation alter membrane potential and neurotransmitter release?
options: Light lowers cGMP, closes Na+ channels, hyperpolarizes, and reduces glutamate release
Light opens voltage-gated Na+ channels and depolarizes rods to about +40 mV
Photoreceptors fire rapid all-or-none action potentials at 500 Hz in bright light
Light increases intracellular cGMP tenfold and thereby depolarizes the receptor
questions.explain: Unlike cutaneous mechanoreceptors or hair cells that depolarize when stimulated, retinal rods and cones hyperpolarize in response to light.

open.q: Explain why vertebrate retinal photoreceptors hyperpolarize rather than depolarize when exposed to light.
accept: Light activates transducin and cGMP phosphodiesterase, lowering intracellular cGMP and closing constitutively open cGMP-gated Na+/Ca2+ channels that maintain the depolarized dark current
Light-induced cGMP breakdown closes Na+ channels, hyperpolarizing the cell

questions.sub: Sensory Transduction, Receptor Potential, and Adaptation
questions.q: In cochlear and vestibular hair cells, how does mechanical deflection of stereocilia toward the tallest stereocilium (kinocilium) produce receptor depolarization?
options: Tip links pull channels open; high endolymph K+ and +80 mV potential drive K+ inward
Deflection closes all Na+ channels and hyperpolarizes the hair cell to about -110 mV
Stereocilia secrete acetylcholine directly into the potassium-rich endolymph fluid
Deflection toward the shortest stereocilium causes depolarization and transmitter release
questions.explain: Because cochlear endolymph has uniquely high [K+] (~150 mM) and a +80 mV endocochlear potential, opening apical mechanotransduction channels drives K+ INTO the hair cell to depolarize it!

open.q: Why does opening apical cation channels in cochlear hair cells cause potassium (K+) INFLUX and depolarization rather than K+ efflux?
accept: The surrounding endolymph has a very high K+ concentration (~150 mM) and a +80 mV positive endocochlear potential, creating a strong electrochemical gradient driving K+ into the negatively charged hair cell
High endolymph [K+] and the +80 mV endocochlear potential drive K+ inward into the cell

questions.sub: Cutaneous Mechanoreceptors and Somatosensory Coding
questions.q: Why is two-point discrimination threshold smallest on the fingertips and lips (~1-3 mm) and largest on the back or thigh (~40-70 mm)?
options: High receptor density, small fields, low convergence, large S1 representation
The back contains no tactile receptors whatsoever in the human integument
Action potentials travel 100 times faster from the fingertips than from the back
Fingertips rely solely on unmyelinated C fibers to transduce fine touch stimuli
questions.explain: High receptor density + small receptive fields + low convergence = high spatial resolution and large cortical magnification on the postcentral gyrus.

open.q: State three neuroanatomical factors responsible for the tiny two-point discrimination threshold (~2 mm) on the human fingertips.
accept: High density of mechanoreceptors (Merkel/Meissner), small receptive fields, low convergence onto ascending neurons, and large cortical representation in S1
High receptor density, small receptive fields, and large S1 cortical magnification

questions.sub: Nociceptors, Thermoreceptors, and Pain Modulation
questions.q: Which transient receptor potential (TRP) ion channels on free nerve endings transduce noxious heat/capsaicin versus innocuous cool/menthol?
options: TRPV1 for noxious heat and capsaicin; TRPM8 for cool and menthol
TRPV1 transduces ice-cold temperatures; TRPM8 transduces boiling water
Both TRPV1 and TRPM8 are voltage-gated sodium channels, not TRP channels
TRPV1 is found exclusively in the retina for phototransduction of light stimuli
questions.explain: Discovery of TRPV1 and Piezo1/Piezo2 mechanosensitive channels earned the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

open.q: Name the TRP receptor channel activated by noxious heat (>43 C) and capsaicin, and the TRP channel activated by cool temperatures and menthol.
accept: TRPV1 (noxious heat and capsaicin) and TRPM8 (cool temperatures and menthol)
TRPV1 and TRPM8

questions.sub: Nociceptors, Thermoreceptors, and Pain Modulation
questions.q: How do 'primary hyperalgesia' (peripheral sensitization) and 'secondary hyperalgesia / allodynia' (central sensitization) differ following tissue injury?
options: Primary: peripheral sensitization at the injury; secondary: central sensitization in uninjured skin
Primary hyperalgesia means complete absence of pain perception at and around the injury
Allodynia means a severed spinal cord with total loss of all sensory modalities
Prostaglandins block all nociceptor firing and are thereby analgesic at the injury site
questions.explain: In allodynia, normally innocuous touch (via A-beta fibers) is perceived as painful due to dorsal horn central sensitization.

open.q: Distinguish hyperalgesia from allodynia, and contrast peripheral sensitization versus central sensitization.
accept: Hyperalgesia: exaggerated pain response to a normally painful stimulus (driven peripherally by inflammatory mediators lowering nociceptor threshold); Allodynia: pain elicited by a normally non-painful stimulus like light touch (driven centrally by dorsal horn NMDA-mediated central sensitization)
Increased pain to noxious stimuli (hyperalgesia/peripheral sensitization) vs pain from innocuous stimuli (allodynia/central sensitization)

questions.sub: Classification and Properties of Sensory Receptors
questions.q: According to the Erlanger-Gasser (alphabetical) and Lloyd-Hunt (numerical) nerve fiber classifications, which sensory fiber groups have the fastest conduction velocities?
options: A-alpha / Type Ia (fastest); then A-beta, A-delta, and unmyelinated C fibers
Unmyelinated C / Type IV fibers conduct at 120 m/s, faster than A-alpha fibers
A-delta fibers are thicker and faster than A-alpha fibers in the spinal cord
Conduction velocity is identical (about 10 m/s) in all sensory axons in the body
questions.explain: Conduction velocity in myelinated fibers scales linearly with axon diameter (~6 x diameter in micrometers), making proprioceptive Ia/Ib afferents the fastest sensory fibers in the body.

open.q: Rank these sensory fibers from fastest to slowest conduction velocity: C (Type IV), A-beta (Type II), A-alpha (Type Ia), and A-delta (Type III).
accept: A-alpha (Type Ia) > A-beta (Type II) > A-delta (Type III) > C (Type IV)
Ia > II > III > IV

questions.sub: Muscle Spindles and the Stretch (Myotatic) Reflex
questions.q: How do 'dynamic gamma motor neurons' and 'static gamma motor neurons' differentially tune muscle spindle sensitivity?
options: Dynamic gamma targets bag1 (velocity); static gamma targets chain (static length)
Dynamic gamma motor neurons paralyze all extrafusal muscle fibers they innervate
Static gamma neurons innervate Golgi tendon organs rather than intrafusal fibers
Both gamma subtypes completely inhibit Type Ia afferent firing during contraction
questions.explain: Descending reticulospinal and vestibulospinal tracts independently adjust dynamic and static fusimotor (gamma) gain depending on whether a motor task demands rapid velocity damping or steady postural holding.

open.q: Compare the targets and functional effects of dynamic gamma motor neurons versus static gamma motor neurons.
accept: Dynamic gamma neurons innervate dynamic nuclear bag fibers to boost velocity-of-stretch sensitivity; static gamma neurons innervate nuclear chain and static bag fibers to maintain steady length sensitivity
Dynamic gamma -> nuclear bag (velocity sensitivity); static gamma -> nuclear chain (static length sensitivity)

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 64-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with numbness and tingling in a 'stocking-glove' distribution, loss of vibration and joint position sense in his toes, absent Achilles tendon reflexes (even with Jendrassik reinforcement), and a positive Romberg sign (swaying/falling when closing his eyes while standing with feet together). Why does he lose balance specifically when closing his eyes?
options: Visual compensation masks proprioceptive loss; eye closure unmasks sensory ataxia
He has a cerebellar vermis tumor that causes ataxia even with eyes open
He has an acute middle cerebral artery stroke causing spastic hyperreflexia
Closing his eyes causes acute hypoglycemia and thereby sudden loss of balance
questions.explain: A positive Romberg sign specifically diagnoses sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia (dorsal column or large-fiber sensory neuropathy), whereas cerebellar ataxia causes instability with eyes BOTH open and closed.

open.q: What does a positive Romberg sign indicate neuroanatomically, and how does it distinguish sensory ataxia from cerebellar ataxia?
accept: Proprioceptive sensory loss (dorsal column-medial lemniscus or large-fiber peripheral neuropathy); in sensory ataxia, vision compensates when eyes are open so instability appears only when eyes close, whereas cerebellar ataxia causes instability with eyes both open and closed
Proprioceptive/dorsal column deficit; instability only with eyes closed (sensory) vs eyes open and closed (cerebellar)

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 58-year-old woman suffers an ischemic stroke in the right internal capsule. Three weeks later, neurological examination of her LEFT upper and lower limbs reveals increased velocity-dependent resistance to passive stretch (spasticity), 4+ hyperactive biceps and patellar reflexes, sustained left ankle clonus, and a left extensor plantar (Babinski) response. Why do deep tendon reflexes become hyperactive after an internal capsule stroke?
options: Loss of descending corticospinal inhibition raises gamma gain and stretch reflex excitability
The stroke directly stimulated left ventral horn alpha motor neurons in the spinal cord
Peripheral Type Ia sensory axons grew twice as thick after the stroke as a compensation
Golgi tendon organs were destroyed in the left leg by the stroke's vascular territory
questions.explain: Capsular lesions interrupt both corticospinal and corticoreticular fibers, disinhibiting facilitatory medullary/pontine reticulospinal drive to spinal stretch reflex circuits.

open.q: Explain why an upper motor neuron lesion in the internal capsule produces contralateral hyperreflexia and spasticity.
accept: Interruption of descending inhibitory corticospinal/corticoreticular tracts disinhibits spinal gamma and alpha motor neurons and reduces Ia presynaptic inhibition, exaggerating the stretch reflex
Loss of descending inhibitory control over spinal stretch reflex arcs and gamma motor neurons

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 46-year-old man presents with sharp, shooting lower back pain radiating down the posterior right thigh and lateral calf into the sole of the foot after lifting heavy boxes. Examination reveals weakness of right plantar flexion, sensory loss over the lateral foot, and an ABSENT right Achilles tendon reflex, while the right patellar reflex is normal (2+). Which nerve root is compressed?
options: Right S1 nerve root (usually an L5-S1 disc herniation)
Right L3 nerve root (usually an L2-L3 disc herniation)
Right C7 nerve root (usually a C6-C7 disc herniation)
Left L4 nerve root (usually an L3-L4 disc herniation)
questions.explain: An L5-S1 disc herniation compresses the traversing S1 nerve root, interrupting the S1 afferent/efferent limb of the Achilles reflex (LMN radiculopathy).

open.q: Which spinal nerve root and intervertebral disc level are most likely affected in a patient with posterior leg sciatica, weak plantar flexion, lateral foot numbness, and an absent Achilles reflex?
accept: S1 nerve root (L5-S1 intervertebral disc herniation)
S1 root / L5-S1 disc

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 35-year-old gardener steps on a rusty nail and develops severe painful jaw spasms (trismus), arched back (opisthotonos), and generalized muscle spasms triggered by minor sounds or touch 7 days later. How does Clostridium tetani toxin (tetanospasmin) produce these violent spasms?
options: Tetanospasmin blocks central glycine/GABA release, causing spastic co-contraction
Tetanospasmin blocks acetylcholine release at the NMJ, causing flaccid paralysis
Tetanospasmin destroys Type Ia sensory receptors inside the muscle spindles
Tetanospasmin blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels in peripheral sensory nerve fibers
questions.explain: Whereas botulinum toxin acts peripherally at the NMJ to block ACh release (flaccid paralysis), tetanospasmin acts centrally in the spinal cord to block inhibitory glycine/GABA release from Renshaw and Ia interneurons (spastic tetanic paralysis).

open.q: Contrast the sites of action and clinical motor effects of tetanus toxin versus botulinum toxin.
accept: Tetanus toxin acts centrally in the spinal cord/brainstem to block inhibitory glycine and GABA release from Renshaw/inhibitory interneurons (causing spastic paralysis/tetany); Botulinum toxin acts peripherally at the neuromuscular junction to block acetylcholine release (causing flaccid paralysis)
Central glycine/GABA blockade -> spastic paralysis (tetanus) vs peripheral NMJ ACh blockade -> flaccid paralysis (botulinum)

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 28-year-old woman sustains a traumatic hemisection of the right half of the spinal cord at T8 (Brown-Sequard syndrome) from a knife wound. Three months later, what sensory and reflex deficits are present BELOW the T8 level?
options: Ipsilateral spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, dorsal column loss; contralateral pain/temperature loss
Bilateral flaccid paralysis of both arms with completely intact strength in both legs
Contralateral loss of vibration and ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature only
Complete absence of all spinal reflexes above the fifth cervical cord segment
questions.explain: Because dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts decussate in the medulla while spinothalamic axons ascend 1-2 segments in Lissauer's tract before decussating in the anterior white commissure, hemisection produces ipsilateral UMN + dorsal column loss and contralateral spinothalamic loss.

open.q: Summarize the motor, reflex, and sensory deficits beneath the lesion in a right-sided T8 spinal cord hemisection (Brown-Sequard syndrome).
accept: Ipsilateral (right) UMN spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign, and loss of proprioception/vibration/fine touch below T8; contralateral (left) loss of pain and temperature starting 1-2 segments below T8
Ipsilateral UMN weakness/hyperreflexia and dorsal column loss + contralateral spinothalamic pain/temperature loss

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with acute substernal chest tightness radiating down the medial aspect of his left arm and into his jaw during exertion, accompanied by diaphoresis and ST-segment elevations on ECG. Why is cardiac ischemic pain perceived in the left C8-T1 dermatome (medial arm)?
options: Cardiac T1-T5 afferents converge with somatic C8-T1 afferents on shared spinothalamic neurons
Coronary arteries run directly down the left brachial plexus and carry pain fibers
The phrenic nerve innervates the skin of the left hand, referring pain to that area
Myocardial ischemia stimulates Pacinian corpuscles in the palm via local mediators
questions.explain: Convergence of T1-T5 cardiac sympathetic visceral afferents with T1-T4 somatic cutaneous afferents in the spinal dorsal horn causes the somatosensory cortex to project cardiac pain onto the chest and medial left arm.

open.q: Identify the spinal cord segments and afferent pathway responsible for referring myocardial ischemic pain to the chest wall and medial left arm.
accept: T1-T5 (especially T1-T4) spinal segments via cardiac sympathetic visceral nociceptive afferents converging with T1-T4 somatic afferents on shared spinothalamic dorsal horn neurons
T1-T5 cardiac sympathetic afferents converging with somatic afferents in the dorsal horn
